title: Why Fig Newtons Are Named After A Town
sources: Wikipedia, 'Newtons (cookie)' (invented by Charles Roser; first baked 1891 at the F. A. Kennedy Steam Bakery, Cambridgeport, Massachusetts; plant manager James Hazen named it after the Boston suburb of Newton, Massachusetts)
UPI, 'The Fig Newton turns 100' (1991): Kennedy plant manager James Hazen had a penchant for naming new cookies after Massachusetts cities and towns; he named the fig creation the Newton
WBSM / ThoughtCo: the company had a habit of naming cookies after local towns and already had cookies named Beacon Hill, Harvard and Shrewsbury when the Newton was created
Straight Dope, 'Who or what are Fig Newton cookies named after?' (Nabisco: Kennedy Biscuit named all their products after surrounding communities, including 'Shrewsbury', 'Harvard', 'Beacon Hill')
GBH / History Cambridge (Jan 2026): not named for Sir Isaac Newton; Kennedy already had cookies and pastries named for local places
Caveat: Nabisco's own line is that the name came from 'either Sir Isaac Newton or the town of Newton'; historians and local sources say the town. Script says 'a habit', not 'all' of its cookies.

lines.text: Lots of people think Fig Newtons were named after Isaac Newton, the apple guy.
But nope, they're named after a town in Massachusetts.
See, back in 1891, a man named Charles Roser
